title: Boost Your Resume with Quantifiable Achievements to Stand out in Hiring
author: Emmanuel Adams
content:
As a seasoned business and fintech consultant, deeply involved in career development, I consistently advocate for the integration of robust metrics within professional resumes. This isn’t merely a stylistic preference; it’s a strategic imperative that yields multiple benefits:

Aligning with Business Acumen:
 The corporate world operates on data, key performance indicators (KPIs), and return on investment (ROI). By presenting your career narrative through a lens of quantitative outcomes, you inherently speak the language of business, resonating powerfully with decision-makers seeking results-oriented professionals.

Bolstering Credibility:
 Numerical data provides irrefutable, objective evidence of your capabilities, transcending subjective claims and establishing a foundation of trust.

Exemplifying Expertise:
 The ability to quantify your impact signifies a profound grasp of your functional domain and an acute awareness of organizational objectives. It highlights your strategic foresight and capacity for delivering measurable results.

Demonstrating Tangible Impact:
 Metrics directly illustrate the positive transformations you have initiated or contributed to, whether through enhanced efficiency, revenue generation, cost reduction, or complex problem resolution. This precise demonstration enables prospective employers to immediately perceive your potential contribution to their enterprise.

A Structured Approach to Quantifying Your Contributions: The “Before & After” Analytical Framework

Many professionals grapple with the challenge of assigning numerical values to their work. If you’re in this position, I propose a systematic “Before & After” analytical framework designed to extract and articulate your quantifiable achievements:

Phase 1: Pre-Intervention Analysis (The “Before” State)
 Commence by meticulously recalling the prevailing conditions or performance metrics prior to your involvement or the initiation of your work. Detail the environment or situation from a baseline perspective:

What was the average duration or lead time for a particular process?

What was the initial customer satisfaction score or feedback trend?

How many personnel comprised the team, or what was the scope of the project?

Identify and document existing inefficiencies, bottlenecks, or unresolved challenges.

Ascertain the initial status quo or benchmark performance level.

Phase 2: Post-Intervention Assessment (The “After” State)
 Subsequently, delineate the situation or performance indicators 
following
 the completion of your work or the implementation of your solutions. Describe the outcomes and improvements:

By what percentage or factor was the process expedited or streamlined?

What observable improvements were registered in terms of quality, throughput, or operational speed?

Did your initiatives lead to an expansion in budget, team size, client portfolio, or top-line revenue?

Which specific impediments were effectively surmounted, or which issues were significantly ameliorated?

Articulate the newly established performance standard or improved status.

Phase 3: Deriving Quantifiable Achievements
 Scrutinize both lists for common units of measurement or discernible correlations between the pre- and post-intervention states. These quantifiable units could encompass time, financial figures, percentages, headcount, customer satisfaction indices, error rates, or compliance adherence.

The identification of these common denominators will empower you to calculate the precise magnitude of your impact, often expressed as percentages or absolute figures. The presence of percentages directly translates into compelling, quantifiable achievements ready for your resume.

Illustrative Case Studies:

Example 1: Process Efficiency (Human Resources/Operations)

Initial State:
 “The average onboarding process for new hires took 15 business days, involving manual data entry across multiple departments.”

Outcome State:
 “After implementing a new digital workflow and cross-functional training, the average onboarding process was reduced to 3 business days.”

Articulated Quantifiable Achievement:
 “Streamlined the new hire onboarding process, reducing completion time by 
80%
 (from 15 to 3 days) through digital workflow integration, enhancing efficiency for over 50 new hires annually.”

Example 2: Revenue Generation (Sales/Business Development)

Initial State:
 “The average monthly conversion rate for inbound sales leads stood at 8%, yielding approximately $50,000 in new monthly revenue.”

Outcome State:
 “Following the optimization of our lead nurturing sequence and sales pitch, the monthly conversion rate increased to 12%, generating $75,000 in new monthly revenue.”

Articulated Quantifiable Achievement:
 “Optimized inbound lead nurturing and sales conversion strategies, increasing the monthly lead conversion rate by 
50%
 (from 8% to 12%) and generating an additional 
$25,000
 in new monthly revenue.”

The diligent application of this framework will transform your resume from a descriptive summary into a compelling testament of your professional efficacy and value generation.

I trust this comprehensive guide will serve as an invaluable resource in refining your professional narrative.

title: Feeling Unmotivated? - Focus on Short-term goals.
author: Chimdinma Onwuegbu
content:
What does success mean to you, and how do you define and measure it? We usually have our eyes set on the ultimate focus and goal which might need a big leap to reach. Most times, that could be tiring. Have you ever tried setting multiple short-term goals towards the long-term goal? 

According  to Roger Federer, You have to believe in the long term plan but you need short-term goals to motivate and and inspire you.

Lets say you have this goal of building a house. Defining success as a fully completed and furnished house might make success seem a long way off. However, setting multiple short-term goals and defining each short-term goal as success will keep you motivated. Short-term goals in this regard could be getting 50 bags of cement or 5 trips of sand, getting the needed rod or planks needed for the job etc. It could also mean setting success as - completion of Foundation, getting the house to lintel level, completing plastering work etc. Seeing each level as a success will keep you inspired.

As a job seeker, the long-term goal will be getting the job of your dream. However, you can set short-term goals that will keep you inspired throughout the journey of job hunting. You can set daily application targets and celebrate meeting the targeted number of applications each day. 

Setting little targets and celebrating each little target met will keep you motivated throughout the journey. With this format, you will keep feeling a sense of accomplishment and be more likely to stay on course till the final goal is achieved.

Have you ever focused on long-term goals without breaking them into short-term goals? What was your experience? Please feel free to share in the comment section.

title: Framing is a very important skill in the corporate sector
author: Chimdinma Onwuegbu
content:
Framing is a very important skill to have in your kitty. This skill becomes even more important if you are working in the corporate sector.

Being direct and blunt will not always work in your favour. It doesnt matter whether you are a superior or not, framing your words appropriately will make you sound more professional, diplomatic, and constructive.

This will be a great boost to your personal and professional brand.

Here are a couple of examples of how to frame your words constructively.

Direct - This is a terrible idea.

Corporate Reframe - I think we should explore some alternative approaches to ensure alignment with our goals.

 Direct - You’re wrong.

Corporate Reframe - I see (or recall) it a bit differently.

Direct - This is taking too long.

Corporate Reframe - Let’s identify ways to streamline this process for efficiency.

Direct - I don’t have time for this.

Corporate Reframe - I’d be happy to help once I wrap up my current priorities.

Direct - That’s not my job.

Corporate Reframe - Let me check who the right point of contact would be for this.

Direct - This meeting is pointless.

Corporate Reframe - Could we clarify the objectives of this meeting to maximize productivity?

Direct - You didn’t do this right.

Corporate Reframe - Let’s review this together to ensure we meet the expected standards.

Direct - I don’t care what they think.

Corporate Reframe - While I understand their perspective, here’s why I recommend a different approach.

9. Direct - Just get it done.

Corporate Reframe - Let’s prioritize this and align on a realistic timeline.

10. Direct - This is a waste of money.

Corporate Reframe - Let’s evaluate the ROI on this to ensure it aligns with our budget priorities.

With the reframe, the message is passed in a subtle and more efficient manner, avoiding the possible psychological and emotional negative impact the direct approach would have had on the reciever.

It's not always about what was said, but about how it was said.

Yours in career progress,

Chimdinma Onwuegbu

title: From Dominance to Decline: How 2go Missed Its Chance to Be Africa’s Social Media Giant
author: Emmanuel Adams
content:
The meteoric rise and eventual decline of 2go across Africa offer a compelling case study in the dynamics of technology adoption, market leadership, and the critical importance of continuous innovation, adaptation, and, as we now understand, dedicated user support in the fast-paced digital landscape.

A South African Genesis, A Pan-African Phenomenon:

The story of 2go begins not in Nigeria, but in 
Johannesburg, South Africa, in 2007
. It was conceived by a group of forward-thinking 
University of Witwatersrand computer science students
 as a students-only mobile website, initially serving as a vital communication tool within their academic community. This grassroots origin laid the foundation for a platform built on connection. 2go eventually evolved beyond its student-exclusive model, setting its sights on the broader, burgeoning mobile markets across Africa, quickly gaining traction in countries like 
Nigeria, Kenya, and Ghana
.

From 2008 to 2012, 2go wasn’t just an application; it was a cultural phenomenon, a digital staple that defined online interaction for millions of young Africans. Its dominance, particularly by 2012 when it overshadowed Facebook with over 12 million users to Facebook’s 6.5 million in Nigeria alone, marked it as the quintessential “cool” app. It boasted features like the ability to add users from chat rooms without sharing personal information and offered a variety of customizable “skins.” This innovation even rivaled the likes of 
Mxit
, a dominant South African social media platform at the time. Being on 2go was a badge of digital sophistication, turning it into a hotspot for students and youth across the continent. The anecdote of a user seamlessly adopting a pre-existing 2go profile underscores the organic, almost viral, nature of its adoption. It wasn’t about meticulous onboarding; it was about being connected, being part of the conversation. For half a decade, 2go reigned supreme, creating a vibrant ecosystem of chat rooms and direct messaging that catered to the communication needs of a rapidly digitizing population.

The Myth of WhatsApp’s Immediate Victory:

A common misconception attributes 2go’s downfall solely to WhatsApp’s emergence. However, a deeper analysis reveals a more nuanced truth. WhatsApp, launched in 2009, two years after 2go gained traction, observed 2go’s supremacy for a considerable period. WhatsApp’s ascendance to the top only truly began when Android smartphones became widely accessible and affordable across Africa. This shift in the hardware landscape exposed 2go’s strategic missteps and highlighted its critical failure to evolve with changing user expectations and technological advancements.

The Fatal Flaws: Failure to Adapt, Innovate, and Support:

2go’s decline wasn’t an overnight collapse but a gradual erosion, starting significantly around 
2018
. Its inability to innovate and adapt was a major factor. Their “lazy porting” of the Java app to Android was a significant strategic blunder. While WhatsApp embraced rich media sharing, allowing users to effortlessly share photos, videos, and create free group chats, 2go remained tethered to its text-centric model. Its paid “GoCredits” for chat rooms, coupled with limited user control, became increasingly unappealing in an era of free, feature-rich alternatives. The progression of video calls around 2018 further highlighted 2go’s technological stagnation, causing it to fall behind and lose the majority of its user base.

However, a deeper, and perhaps more insidious, factor in 2go’s demise was the 
failure of its support team
. As early as 
2020
, the 2go support team unofficially abandoned the platform. They began charging users more for fewer services, consistently failed to fix reported issues, and often resorted to banning user accounts rather than addressing underlying problems. By 
2024
, the support team had gone completely silent. Despite the app remaining active and still requiring costly verifications for users, there was no support left. Issues reported by the few remaining devoted users could take weeks, or even months, to receive a response — if at all. This abandonment led to a critical breakdown of trust and user experience, ultimately driving away even the most loyal adherents. By 
2025
, 2go was little more than a memory, with active users reduced to a near halt, composed only of a handful of the same individuals logging in and out. The consensus among many devoted users is clear: 
2go failed because its support team failed.

The Power of Network Effects and Missed Opportunities:

The core lesson from 2go’s demise, and indeed from the sustained dominance of platforms like WhatsApp, lies in the principle of network effects. Social networks thrive on community. If one’s friends, family, and professional contacts are on a particular platform, the incentive to switch is minimal. Logging into an empty 2go became a pointless exercise, leading to eventual uninstallation. This phenomenon also explains why platforms like Telegram, despite their robust features, have struggled to dethrone WhatsApp in Africa; the established network is simply too entrenched. To incentivize a mass migration, an overwhelmingly compelling reason, such as completely free internet access, would be necessary.

2go’s failure wasn’t limited to its lack of media sharing or its support issues. It also failed to recognize and pivot towards new avenues of user engagement. WhatsApp’s introduction of “Status” features, which allow users to share ephemeral updates, photos, and videos, significantly boosted engagement even when direct messaging activity was low. This foresight kept users within the app’s ecosystem. Had 2go introduced a similar user feed or media status updates, things might have been different. The dream of seeing a homegrown African app dominate globally, as 2go had the potential to do, remained unfulfilled.

The Enduring Legacy and Broader Implications:

The story of 2go, from its student origins in South Africa to its pan-African prominence and eventual collapse, is a poignant reminder of the relentless pace of technological evolution, the unforgiving nature of the digital market, and the absolute necessity of sustained user support. Today, the African social media landscape is overwhelmingly dominated by Western platforms like Facebook, WhatsApp, and Instagram. This dominance raises critical questions about data privacy, digital sovereignty, and the vast amounts of information these platforms collect on African citizens — often more detailed than what local governments possess.

The analogy of 2go as a “mighty iroko tree” that eventually fell powerfully encapsulates its rise and dramatic decline, serving as a cautionary tale for aspiring tech giants across the continent. For entrepreneurs and innovators, the lessons are clear: continuous innovation, genuine adaptability to changing technological landscapes, understanding evolving user needs, leveraging network effects, and, crucially, maintaining a robust and responsive support system are paramount for sustainable success in the dynamic African digital realm.

title: June has been such a blessing!
author: Chimdinma Onwuegbu
content:
My audience consisted of Doctors, Nurses, Biomedical Scientists, Bankers, Lawyers, Students, Engineers, Business owners, Managers etc. I ensured to speak to everyone  in a language that made sense to where they were at the time.
I absolutely love doing data - all of the cleaning, sorting and filtering, wrangling and formating, modelling and relationships, Power pivots and queries, V and X lookups, Visualising with Power-BI, Lux, Matplotlib and Seaborn or keeping it simple with Excel dashboards, employing built in AIs where need be and creating visuals that  tell meaningful stories while providing insights. I love the thrill that comes with having to reject or failing to uphold a hypothesis based on statistical revelations. 
I love all of that.

Having spent the last couple of weekends talking to hundreads of people about data, I have come to the conclusion that talking about data is just as exciting as doing data.  Sharing my knowledge and insights with colleagues, friends, acquaintances and even total strangers has been such a blessing.
Being part of the success story of many who I may never meet in person has been an honor. 
Talking, sharing, connecting. 
This month has shown me that the little you know might be a big deal to someone else and the more you share knowledge, you leave an indelible print of you in the hearts of people and collectively we make the world a better place.
My verbal and non verbal communication skills, presentation and delivery as well as audience capture capacity has grown and I am thrilled!!!
June has been such a blessing!
I am a self-motivated Data Analyst and Communicator. I am evolving and I am so loving me.
Wishing you a fantastic week filled with blessings and so much love 

❤️ 😍 

 
Chimdinma Onwuegbu
founder 
Precheks Consulting

title: Making a career change in your 30s, 40s, or 50s  - A career crisis or upgrade
author: Chimdinma Onwuegbu
content:
In Your 30s, 40s, or 50s, making a career change in your 3 can either result in a career crisis or career upgrade.

At this time, you might have already put in at least a decade of your life into your current career path and settling into a phase of acceptable stability.

Pivoting now would might seem like upsetting status quo and stepping out of your career comfort zone.

A few years ago, in my 30s, I did something similar.

I had built a career as a medical laboratory scientist with over a decade's worth of hands on experience in the wet lab and classroom. I did not just practice medical laboratory science, I taught same in the Univeristy and College of Health.

I was good at it. I loved the profession. I still do.

When my priorities changed a couple of years ago and a career pivot became imminent, I did what most people only think about — I made a change.

I did not make the change because I had it all figured out.

Not at all.

I made the change because I knew choosing the comfort of a career path I was familiar with, that would leave me struggling with other aspects of my life, felt far more dangerous than starting over in a new path that was both flexible and scalable with far less stress in the long run.

Having made this change and guided others to do same, I want to share how you can strategically make a career change without falling into crisis especially if you are in your 30s, 40s or 50s:

 Audit Your Skills & Passions.

At this point in your career, you’re not starting from zero. You’ve built years of expertise, perspective, and instinct from your years of work that could be transferable.

So, ask yourself:

* What do people always come to me for?

* What do I do well that doesn’t drain me?

* What part of my current work do I actually *enjoy?

That’s your foundation — not a clean slate, but a platform.

(For me, it was my ability to analyse different patient investigations, arrive at a logical diagnosis and possible intervention plan and communicate same to the patient, no matter how difficult it was)

Find yours.

Next

 Upskill on the outcome of your audit while still in your current role.

You do not need to acquire tons of new certifications to upskill. You just need one or two. Choose maximum of two new skills that unlocks your next opportunity — something aligned with the result of your audit.

(For me, it was deepening my analytical and communication skills — something that turned out to be my bridge to more meaningful work.)

Find yours.

 Network for Knowledge, Not Jobs

I will not say ignore regular job boards like LinkedIn or Indeed but real gold is in having conversations with actual people and building relationships.

Talk to people already in the space you’re curious about. Ask how they got in, what they’d do differently, and what skills matter most.

Some opportunities aren’t listed. They’re shared.

 Take small bets on yourself.

You don’t need to leap without a parachute.

Test your interest and build credibility through freelance, shadowing, volunteering, consulting part-time etc.

These “small bets” give you proof of concept, builds your confidence and competencies.

For me, I started recreating dashboards I saw online, mirroring descriptive and exploratory analysis of people already in the field and playing around with any dataset I could find.

 5. Start Before You Feel Ready

Imposter syndrome is real whem it comes to career pivot. However, you must know that Imposter syndrome doesn’t mean you’re unqualified or incompetent. It means you’re growing because questioning your capability and finding the answer leads to growth.

Nobody feels 100% ready for a career pivot.

How do you start?

Start seeing yourself as a professional in the path you are aspiring to, use the terminologies and jargons, create and build a brand to reflect the new you, sell your brand with every opportunity you get.

In no time, Imposter syndrome will take a flight.

Midlife career change does not call for drastic actions but strategic ones.

This isn’t about quitting your job overnight.

It’s about designing a career — and life — that actually fits who you are becoming.

So, Rethink, Reframe, Realign.

Yours in career progress

Chimdinma Onwuegbu

title: Minding the Pay Gap:
author: Chimdinma Onwuegbu
content:
Why Pay Transparency Isn't Just a Buzzword, It's a Business Imperative

For decades, the conversation around pay gaps—be they based on gender, race, or other demographic factors—has persisted as a stubborn feature of the global economic landscape. While progress has been made, the gaps remain, silently undermining organizational health, eroding trust, and hampering innovation. The traditional approach of acknowledging the problem in broad strokes is no longer sufficient. To truly forge a path to equity, we must embrace a more rigorous, three-step mandate: make the data visible, reflect on its stark realities, and fundamentally re-engineer how we construct and present compensation offers.

1. The Data Deficit: Seeing is Believing

The first and most formidable barrier to closing the pay gap is obscurity. Compensation has long been shrouded in a culture of secrecy, a practice defended as a means to prevent employee dissatisfaction and maintain a competitive edge.
 In reality, this opacity primarily serves to protect outdated and often biased pay structures. Without clear, accessible data, the pay gap remains an abstract concept, easily dismissed or underestimated.

The call for more data to be 
seen
 is a call for radical transparency. This involves:

Internal Audits:
 Conducting regular, thorough analyses of compensation across the entire organization. This data must be segmented not just by role and seniority, but by gender, race, ethnicity, and other demographics to reveal the often-hidden intersectional disparities.

External Reporting:
 Increasingly, jurisdictions across the globe are mandating pay transparency. Companies in the EU and several US states are now required to report on their gender pay gaps. Proactive organizations should not wait for legislation; they should lead by voluntarily reporting their data. This act of transparency is a powerful statement of accountability to employees, investors, and customers.

When data is brought into the light, it shifts the conversation from anecdotal evidence to empirical fact. It establishes a baseline reality, dispels myths, and creates an undeniable impetus for action. You cannot fix a problem you refuse to measure.

2. From Data to Dialogue: The Power of Reflection

Data, on its own, is merely a collection of numbers. Its true power is unlocked when it is 
reflected on
. This is perhaps the most difficult step, as it requires organizations to hold up a mirror to their own practices and confront uncomfortable truths.

Reflection is not a passive activity; it is an active diagnosis. Leaders must ask probing questions:

Where do the disparities originate?
 Are they present in starting salaries, indicating a biased negotiation or offer process? Do they widen over time, suggesting inequitable promotion pathways or biased performance reviews?

Are our job leveling and salary bands consistent and objective?
 Or do roles predominantly held by certain demographics have systematically lower pay ranges for comparable work?

How does unconscious bias manifest in our managers' decisions regarding raises and bonuses?

This process cannot be siloed within the Human Resources department. It must be a strategic conversation at the board and executive levels. It involves critically examining the entire talent lifecycle—from recruitment and hiring to performance management and succession planning. This deep reflection transforms raw data into actionable insights, moving the organization from acknowledging a problem to understanding its root causes.

3. Re-engineering the Offer: A Blueprint for Change

Understanding the problem is essential, but solving it requires a fundamental change in our actions. The final step is to use these insights to redesign the very mechanics of how compensation is determined and offered. The traditional model, often reliant on a candidate's salary history and negotiation prowess, is a primary driver in perpetuating pay gaps.

A forward-thinking approach to compensation offers must include:

Banning Salary History Inquiries:
 Asking for a candidate's previous salary anchors their future earnings to the past, effectively importing any inequities they may have previously experienced. This practice must be abolished.

Implementing Clear Salary Bands:
 Every role should have a well-defined salary range based on objective market data, required skills, and internal equity. These bands should be made transparent to candidates and employees, providing a clear framework for compensation discussions.

Standardizing Offers:
 Instead of starting negotiations low, companies should make their best offer first, based on the candidate's skills and experience as they map to the pre-defined salary band. This levels the playing field, as studies show that the "negotiation-first" model disproportionately disadvantages women and minority groups.

Regular Equity Audits:
 Pay equity should be treated like any other critical business metric. Just as we conduct financial audits, we must conduct regular, scheduled pay equity audits to catch and correct disparities as they arise, not years after the damage has been done.

Conclusion: The ROI of Equity

Closing the pay gap is not merely a matter of social justice or corporate responsibility; it is a profound business and economic imperative. Organizations that lead on pay equity will attract and retain top-tier talent, foster a culture of trust and psychological safety, and unlock greater innovation from a truly diverse workforce. The path forward requires courage—the courage to make data transparent, the humility to reflect on what it tells us, and the conviction to change long-standing practices. By seeing the numbers, reflecting on their meaning, and redesigning our offers, we can finally begin to mind the gap and build organizations that are not only more equitable but also more resilient and successful for it.

title: Nigeria's Youth: The Brain Drain to Content Creation and Gig Work
author: Chimdinma Onwuegbu
content:
Trading brains for buzz and influence?
Lately, I’ve noticed something that’s both interesting and a little worrying.
More and more Nigerian youths are gravitating toward content creation — mostly the non-intellectual kind — and virtual assistant jobs. On the surface, it looks like a win: people are getting creative, making money online, and finding flexible ways to survive in a very difficult economy.
Honestly, I respect the hustle. Nigeria isn’t exactly the easiest place to thrive or survive and I’ll always applaud people doing what they can to make ends meet.
But here’s where my concern kicks in: fewer young people seem to be interested in mainstream academics or intellectually demanding careers. Degrees are getting side-lined, and this is not about the kind of side-lining that comes from critical reflection — it’s more out of frustration and survival.

So what does this mean for us in the long run?
Winning the hustle but losing sight of the bigger picture.
Before I go further, let me be clear: this is not an attack on content creators or virtual assistants. I actually admire people who’ve found ways to thrive in the digital economy. Many of them are creative, hardworking, and resourceful beyond belief.
But I’m also noticing that a large chunk of the content being created today lean heavily toward entertainment and trends — dances, pranks, gossip, and lifestyle hype. While these have their place, they’re not the kind of output that build intellectual capital or challenge how we think. When majority of our youth population start prioritising this over intellectual development, we may be heading into risky territory.

Let’s be honest — it’s easier to go viral for something flashy than for publishing a well-researched article or winning a science competition. Fame and clout are more instantly rewarding than grades or degrees. Academic work involves far more grit and resilience than skits and pranks yet one who excels academically, graduating top of their class, gets far less validation and reward compared to one whose skit or dance video goes viral or better still one who wins BBN or like competitions.

So, What’s Driving This Shift?
Economic Pressure!
Let’s not sugar-coat it — there’s a lot of hardship in Nigeria today. Graduates are doing everything right and still not finding jobs. Those who get jobs are grossly underpaid. These youths come from homes where their parents gave their all to see them through school, yet Nigeria is happening to them. So if someone can earn a bit of money online to make their lives easier, why wouldn’t they?
A Failing Education System!
From the secondary to university level, Nigerian education system is flawed. Students are losing trust in the system. Gaining admission into a Nigerian university seems like an extreme sport. The recent issue with JAMB is a case in-hand. Mainstream education seem to have lost its flavour to the average Nigerian. Many universities in Nigeria haven’t updated their curricula in years. Students get the same academic content year on year. The constant ASUU strikes and lack of real-world relevance in the classroom have left students disillusioned. A 4-yr course could drag on for 6yrs or more. Why would anyone want to get entangled with that only to come out and find no good jobs?

Social Media Validation
Let’s be honest — it’s easier to go viral for something flashy than for publishing a well-researched article or winning a science competition. Fame and clout are more instantly rewarding than grades or degrees. Academic work involves far more grit and resilience than skits and pranks yet one who excels academically, graduating top of their class, gets far less validation and reward compared to one whose skit or dance video goes viral or better still one who wins BBN or like competitions.

So What Can We Do About It?
We need to create a system that makes intellectual growth valuable again — financially, socially, and emotionally by fixing our education system. It needs to evolve. Courses should reflect the digital age. Learning should be digitised, interactive and practical. Schools should work with industries to bridge the gap between digital and intellectual work.
Content creation and academia do not have to be separate worlds. Why can’t a young Nigerian go viral for breaking down public policy or sharing research-backed health tips in a creative way or building a data integration model to centralise our national database?
We need to intentionally and optimally showcase smart role models. Let’s give flowers to people doing intellectually cool work. Analysts, engineers, doctors, and thought leaders who are making impact and income — youths need to see that success can also come from knowledge. Sponsors of BBN and their likes should seek out intellectually cool Nigerians and give them such life lifts so that those fellows can act as mentors to younger Nigerians. We need more initiatives that pair young people with accomplished mentors in high-impact sectors.
Many youths simply don’t know what’s possible because no one has shown them. I know this from my interactions with my clients who are 90% Nigerians.
Like I mentioned at the beginning, this isn’t a “bash the content creators” article— it’s a call for balance. We need thinkers and creators. Hustlers and scholars. There’s no rule that says a young Nigerian can’t be both digitally savvy and intellectually grounded.
So yes, create. Hustle. Build that online brand. But also — read. Learn. Think deeply. Because the Nigeria we dream of won’t just be built by trends. It’ll be built by intellectual minds.

Like I mentioned at the beginning, this isn’t a “bash the content creators” article— it’s a call for balance. We need thinkers and creators. Hustlers and scholars. There’s no rule that says a young Nigerian can’t be both digitally savvy and intellectually grounded.
So yes, create. Hustle. Build that online brand. But also — read. Learn. Think deeply. Because the Nigeria we dream of won’t just be built by trends. It’ll be built by intellectual minds.

Accessibility of Remote Work
Anyone with a smartphone and some basic training can become a VA, run an Instagram page, or edit TikTok videos. These paths are visible, relatively easy to enter, and don’t require years in school. Unfortunately, most mainstream roles in Nigeria are yet to embrace flexible working. This greatly impacts those who have young families or would prefer to work from anywhere but a traditional office.
While these online paths can offer short-term relief, there are long-term consequences we should start talking about:
Loss of Deep Thinkers :
 Who’s going to solve our public health crises, build tech infrastructure, or rewrite policy if fewer people are engaging with complex, intellectual fields? How do we intend to survive without researchers, intrapreneurs, and intellectuals?
Overdependence on Gig Work :
 Many VA or content jobs don’t offer stability, benefits, or growth. They do not control their job because if any of the social media platforms where they have majority of their followings crashes or locks them out, they become jobless instantly. Since they might not have developed their content creation into core skills, they struggle to fit into the real world.
Erosion of Knowledge Culture :
 If we stop valuing education, even in informal ways, we risk losing a culture of curiosity, innovation, and critical thinking. We end up raising people who are alien to intellectual depth but thrive on the euphoria of trends and fame. Fame fades. Trends change. And when there’s no solid skillset, academic foundation or knowledge quest, it becomes hard to pivot when the algorithm isn’t on your side anymore.

Written by 
Chimdinma Onwuegbu

title: Self-Doubt! Imposter Syndrome!!
author: Chimdinma Onwuegbu
content:
Self-Doubt! Imposter Syndrome!!

Lack of Faith in You!!!
Have you ever experienced any of these?
 I have.
The most recent was my time at Leeds Beckett University. I had completed all courses, concluded my project and handed in my dissertation, awaiting the final result. 
I had put in my best during the study time and was aiming for a distinction as my final grade.

As an international student, I was first challenged with being away from my children and family and finding a balance between work and school. 

When my family joined me, the challenges escalated to dealing with school run, cooking, cleaning, work and also school. 

To make matters worse, I got pregnant!!😄
Morning sickness, extreme fatigue, hormonal riots joined the mix of challenges. 

Along the line, towards the end of my study time, I started doubting if I would make a distinction. I told myself that a Merit was just as good because I did not think that with all that I was juggling at the same time, that I deserved a distinction.

When the final results were published, I looked at the result in shock and disbelief!
I did not believe what I saw.

I looked at my name and student number several times to be sure what I was seeing was mine.

It was written clearly  - Final Grade - Distinction!!!

I lived in doubt for weeks as I kept thinking this could be an error but it wasn't. I wrote my academic supervisor, thanking her for all her support and how I could not believe my result.
In her words - You worked hard for this. You deserve it. This is all you. Congratulations!!
Then it sank in. I told myself that I got that because I deserved it. That was the last of Self-doubt and lack of Faith.
Dear Friend, you deserve whatever you work hard for. So when the results come in and look better than you expected, give yourself a pat on the back. Celebrate yourself. You deserve it and more.
Ditch the self-doubt and take a deserved  bow.
You are a success!!
I love you❤️❤️

Chimdinma Onwuegbu
founder

title: Skill is Key!
author: Chimdinma Onwuegbu
content:
Skill is Key 🔑

One of the things I learnt while earning a degree abroad is that people do not get a degree because they want to get a better job or become wealthy.
This is because with or without a degree, you can still have access to all the good things of life - buy a good car, buy a house, get married, have children, travel to premium holiday destinations etc.

Infact, when I was studying for my M.Sc and working part-time as a support worker, I came to work straight from school looking all tired. My manager looked me in the face and asked me why I bother with going to university. She did not see any reason why I had to put myself through all that stress. According to her, she'd never do it. She was just 23 with a good car and saving up to buy a house.

The essence of a university education is to improve on your ability to think critically, broadly and rationally so that you can come with fresh ideas, theories and policies that will better the society. Acquiring a degree is not designed to be a means to wealth. Most of my university professors and PhD holders have no airs around them. They would pass you and you would never know. They are not rich.

In a couple of days, I would be sitting on an interview panel to hire a data analyst into a sister team of my department, and going through the applications, some of the applicants are PhD holders.
I do not have a PhD but I am already occupying the position they are aspiring for and even a level higher.
They won't be treated differently or automatically given the role because they have a PhD but we are hoping that having studied to that level, their approach to business issues will be different.

What am I trying to say?
If the reason you are clamouring to go to Uni is because you want to make more money, you have the wrong reason.
Go acquire a skill and make money.
This mindset is why there are many unemployable graduates. Graduates who should naturally be artisans and excelling at it, wasting years in Uni and coming out no better than they were before gaining admission, save for a certificate which in the light of recent happenings could be gotten from any vendor.
Be informed. Stay positive
I love you always❤️❤️
Chimdinma Onwuegbu
founder 
Precheks Consulting

title: The Audacity of Hope...
author: Chimdinma Onwuegbu
content:
A couple of weeks back, during a chat, someone called me "madam motivation" and went on to say that I sell hope in most of my posts. I smiled and gave the "lol" response.
During our very hard times years back, my husband had this simple quote that kept us going. We went through loads of awful experiences with each one looking like the worst till one worse than what we thought was the worst overtook it😀😀. 
So, everytime we hit what seemed like rock bottom, he would voice his famous quote and that will keep us going.
What was that quote -

All we have is hope. The day we stop hoping, we start dying. The day we lose hope, we die

I saw him hang on to dear hope day after day. I saw him live that quote one awful experience after another.
I was the one doing all the (visible) praying, he was the one with unflinching hope and lofty audacious plans.

Hope - the belief, desire, faith and expectation that something will happen.
Why do people commit suuccaaiide?
They lost HOPE! 
That's the only reason.
Hope gives you the audacity to look into a bleak future and smile.
Hope gives you the opportunity to get up and go again.
Hope places an expectation on tomorrow, thus giving you something to look forward to.
When you are at your lowest, hope gives you the audacity to say - my tomorrow must be greater than today.

So, ladies and gentlemen, I proudly sell HOPE. 
If I sold a little of hope in 2023, in 2024, I am going to sell it even more.
If you remain in my space, get ready!
I will be so audacious in selling hope because all of our lives depend on it.
The day we stop hoping, we start dying.
My name is 
Chimdinma Onwuegbu
 and I sell H.O.P.E ❤️

title: What does a fulfilling career mean?
author: Chimdinma Onwuegbu
content:
What does a successful career life look like?

How do you define it?

To answer this question on "What does a fulfilling career mean?", you might probably begin to think about notable names like Dr 
Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala
, Tony Elumelu
 or 
Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
 and you are neither wrong nor right.

These people and more like them have made a name in their respective fields and deserve their flowers. I give it to them.

However, one thing you should never lose sight of is the fact that success is personal. Very personal.

Therefore, you define what a successful career or business life means to you. You set your own success KPI and you determine when it is met or not.

I wrote an article a while ago about your career not being defined by a single role but a sum of all the things you have done and not done in your life.

You don't just wake up and one day to discover that you have a thriving career . You don't stumble on a fulfilling career like you would a job on a job listing board.

No.

You build it. You build a career life that works for YOU.

It is ok to want to be like someone you admire but it is important that your admiration for them drives you to make career decisions that work FOR YOU.

So, you build a successful career -

With personal values that reflect who you are and a vision of who are becoming.

With intentional choices that guide your actions.

With a personal and professional brand created to portray who you are becoming.

From my personal reflections and interactions with others, I have found out that no one gets on the journey of a fulfilling career with 100% certainty.

No, not one.

The active ingredient needed by every one is clarity. You don’t need to know your final destination, but you do need to know what matters to you: the values you won’t compromise on, the kind of work that energises you, the impact you want to have, the kind of life you want to live.

When you gain clarity on these, it will determine how you treat roles. You will be intentional about -

What kind of roles to take on or not.

 How you treat the roles you do take on.

Producing results that reflect your values, serve your vision and support your brand.

When you gain clarity, you will know when to say N-O to certain offers even if it looks good on paper, because you are building a career and not chasing titles with deep pockets.

When you gain clarity, you will realise that even though your personal values are fixed, your vision might not be realised in one fix. You are allowed to evolve and make detours in bringing your visions to fruition.

Clarity turns your career from something that “happens to you” into something you design —and that shift makes all the difference. You take charge of your career plan, you lead, organise and control.

You steer the ship where so ever you want.

You define and build success on your terms.

That is how you build a fulfilling successful career.

Get a vision, gain clarity and build.

I am rooting for you (and me too
)

Yours in career progress,

Chimdinma Onwuegbu

title: Why do we add visuals to reports?
author: Chimdinma Onwuegbu
content:
Why do we add visuals to reports?  
I mean, our reports can still be meaningful even without pie or bar charts, lines or maps. 
Why do we take on the extra stress of putting the insights drawn from data into visuals then?
The reason might be that it makes it digestible, appealing, relatable and easier to deal with.
Most top management team are not very numeric (apologies to every top management player who is😄🙏). Looking at loads of numbers could be tiring to them. So to effectively communicate, we use visuals.
We are attracted to what we see. Most times,  pictures get more attention than texts and numbers. That's why you would hardly see any advert without a visual - picture, video etc.  
In the visual, the colors are important. The colors pass on a message too.
So when we see a visual, we appreciate it more with colors.

How much color are adding to your life? 
If you do not find life interesting anymore, then convert the texts (worries, disappointments, fights, etc) into visuals (anything that interests you). Add color to it (food, shopping, movie nights, games, etc) and you will see life becoming more interesting.

What can you see about yourself? What does your life visual look like? Is it interactive (with friends, family, colleagues etc) or does not stand alone on the dashboard of life. 
Can't see any visuals of you? 
Not to worry, speak to someone you trust. Get help.

In all you do, have a visual of you and let it be colorful.
